blocks.text: An alternating current (AC) is a sinusoidally varying current, which can be represented by time-dependent sine or cosine functions. The emf of an AC generator is V = Vo sin(wt) (17.1), where V is the voltage at time t, Vo its maximum value and w the angular frequency (Fig 17.1). Similarly, for current, I = Io sin(wt), where I is the instantaneous current and Io its maximum (peak) value.

blocks.title: Alternating current or voltage
blocks.text: A periodically varying current or voltage is alternating if every cycle takes one time period T and has two exactly symmetrical half-cycles, one positive and the other negative.

For a current, the direction reverses after every half-cycle; for a voltage, the polarity reverses after every half-cycle. The amplitude (peak value) is the same in every cycle, but the value changes most rapidly at the zero (crossover) points and most slowly at the peaks.

items: Waveform: the path traced by an alternating quantity plotted against time.
Cycle: one complete set of positive and negative values.
Time period (T): the time to complete one cycle, in seconds.
Frequency (f): the number of cycles per second, in hertz (Hz); f = 1/T.

blocks.text: Average, instantaneous, peak and rms values

The average value of an AC waveform is the arithmetic mean of all its instantaneous values over a stated part of the cycle. Over a complete sine wave (0 to 2 pi) the average is zero, because the positive and negative half-cycles cancel (Fig 17.2). So the average of an AC waveform usually means the average over one half-cycle (0 to pi). It matters in rectification: the output of a rectifier is pulsating DC, and for a full-wave rectified sine wave Iav = 0.637 Io and Vav = 0.637 Vo (2/pi of the peak).

The instantaneous value is the value at any instant: V = Vo sin(wt). Since w = 2 pi / T = 2 pi f, V = Vo sin(2 pi f t), and similarly I = Io sin(2 pi f t) (17.2). The peak (maximum) value, Vo or Io, is the highest value reached in a cycle, the top of the positive half-cycle or the bottom of the negative one. The peak-to-peak value is the distance from the positive peak to the negative peak: Vp-p = 2Vo.

blocks.title: Root-mean-square (rms) value
blocks.text: The rms (effective) value of an alternating current is the value of the steady current that produces the same power (heating effect) in a resistor as the alternating current: Irms = Io / square root of 2 = 0.707 Io (17.3). Similarly Vrms = Vo / square root of 2 = 0.707 Vo (17.4). So the rms current is about 70 per cent of the peak current.

blocks.alt: One cycle of a sine wave of voltage against time, with T/4, T/2, 3T/4 and T marked. Dashed horizontal lines mark the peak Vo and -Vo (red), the rms value 0.707 Vo (green) and the half-cycle average 0.637 Vo (orange); a purple double arrow from -Vo to Vo is labelled peak to peak = 2Vo. Below: V = Vo sin(wt) = Vo sin(2 pi f t); Vrms = Vo/sqrt(2); f = 1/T.
blocks.caption: Values of an alternating voltage (original graph after Figs 17.1 to 17.3).
blocks.long_description: The peak is the highest value; the rms value (0.707 of the peak) is the one that matches a DC supply for heating; the half-cycle average (0.637 of the peak) matters for rectified supplies.

blocks.title: Do you know?
blocks.text: Why is AC better than DC for supply? AC is easy to transmit over long distances, even between cities, without much energy loss (its voltage can be stepped up and down with transformers); DC over very long distances loses electric power.

blocks.title: Point to ponder
blocks.text: High-voltage power lines often crackle and hiss because of corona discharge: the air around the conductor is ionised by the strong electric field, giving a faint glow, radio noise and hissing sounds, especially when the voltage exceeds the breakdown strength of the air.

An alternating current has peak value Io = 17 A and period T = 0.10 s (read from the book's graph). Find the current at t = 0.67 s. Solution: I = Io sin(2 pi t / T). Here t/T = 0.67/0.10 = 6.7, so the current has completed 6 whole cycles and 0.7 of another; the phase is 0.7 x 360 degrees = 252 degrees. sin 252 degrees = -0.951, so I = 17 A x (-0.951) = -16.2 A: a current of 16.2 A in the negative direction.

blocks.title: Example 17.1 in the book
blocks.text: The book works out 2 x 3.14 x 0.67 / 0.1 = 42.1 (radians) but then treats it as 42 degrees and uses sin 42 degrees = 0.917 (sin 42 degrees is actually 0.669), giving I = 15.58 A. With the angle in radians, as the formula requires, I = -16.2 A. Flagged for review.

blocks.title: Do you know?
blocks.text: How can you tell whether a current is alternating? Find the direction of the current and see whether it changes or stays the same: if it periodically reverses, the current is alternating; if it always flows one way, it is direct. A non-contact voltage detector (a pen tester) or a multimeter on its AC setting can even find AC wiring under a carpet by sensing its changing electromagnetic field.

blocks.prompt: The mains voltage in Pakistan is 220 V rms at 50 Hz. What are its peak value, peak-to-peak value and period?
blocks.explanation: Vo = 220 x square root of 2 = 311 V; Vp-p = 2 x 311 = 622 V; T = 1/50 = 0.02 s.

items: V = Vo sin(wt) = Vo sin(2 pi f t); f = 1/T.
rms = peak / sqrt(2) = 0.707 x peak (same heating as DC).
